opus-5.5.text:
I think it's important to be clear-eyed about where the bottleneck actually is. People sometimes talk about AI in drug development as if the hard part is coming up with molecules, and if we could just generate more candidates faster, we'd cure everything. But that's not really the rate-limiting step. Roughly 90% of drugs that enter clinical trials fail, and most of them fail because they don't work in people, or they turn out to be unsafe in ways we didn't anticipate. So the real problem is that our preclinical models, whether cell lines or mice, are just not very predictive of human biology.

The FDA's emphasis on safety is, honestly, appropriate. You're putting a new chemical entity or a new biologic into a human being, and that requires a very high bar. I don't think AI's promise is to get around that bar. I think the promise is to help us clear it more often, and to know earlier which programs are going to clear it.

Where I get excited is the idea of building much better models of human cells and human biology. If you can predict how a cell will respond to a perturbation, whether that's a drug, a genetic edit, or a combination, then you can start to do a lot of the failing in silico instead of in a Phase 2 trial ten years and hundreds of millions of dollars later. That's the vision behind things like a virtual cell. It's not about replacing clinical trials. It's about making sure the things that go into trials have a much higher prior probability of working and being safe.

There's also a regulatory evolution happening that I think is interesting. The FDA has signaled more openness to non-animal methods, things like organoids and computational models, as part of the evidence package. That's a sign that regulators recognize animal models have real limitations too. If AI-driven models can demonstrate that they're actually more predictive of human toxicity or efficacy, I think regulators will increasingly be willing to accept that evidence. But it has to be earned with data. You have to show prospectively that these models work.

So my view is that safety and AI aren't in tension. The best version of AI in drug development is one that makes drugs safer, because we understand the biology better before we ever dose a patient. The near-term wins are probably in target selection, patient stratification, and predicting toxicity. The longer-term, more ambitious goal is being able to simulate biology well enough that we fundamentally change the success rate of the whole enterprise. And if we can move that 90% failure rate even meaningfully, that's an enormous amount of value, both economically and in terms of patients getting medicines that work.

r001.rationale: The response links the high failure rate to poor preclinical models, and separately says the FDA’s safety emphasis is appropriate because dosing people requires a high bar. It does not attribute the FDA’s emphasis to the failure rate.

r002.rationale: The response says AI can raise the probability that programs entering trials will work and be safe, and describes improving the overall success rate as a goal.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. I actually think the FDA's emphasis on safety is the right frame to start from, because it clarifies where AI can and can't help right now.

The thing people get wrong is imagining AI replaces the clinical trial. It won't, and it shouldn't. The trial is the moment where we learn whether a hypothesis about human biology is true, and no model today has a good enough prior on human physiology to skip that. Something like ninety percent of drugs that enter the clinic fail, and most of those failures are because the biology was wrong, not because the chemistry was bad. So if you tell me you've built a model that designs a beautiful molecule, I'll say great, but you've optimized the part of the process that was already working reasonably well.

Where I'm genuinely excited is upstream of that. The real bottleneck is choosing the right target and understanding the mechanism before you commit hundreds of millions of dollars. That's where models trained on genomic sequence, perturbation data, and cellular readouts can change the odds. If you can predict which gene to hit, in which cell type, and what the off-target consequences are, you're not making the trial less rigorous. You're walking into it with a much better hypothesis. That's a safety story as much as an efficiency story.

The second place is in the design of the therapeutic itself, particularly for programmable modalities. With gene editing or RNA therapies, the molecule is essentially software. You can generate thousands of variants, screen them, and learn what makes something more specific and less immunogenic. Specificity is safety. A model that helps you design an editor with fewer off-target cuts is directly serving the thing the FDA cares about.

Then there's the regulatory interface. I think the agency is more open than people assume. They've put out guidance on AI in drug development, they're thinking about how to evaluate model-derived evidence, and they want transparency on what was predicted versus what was measured. If the field treats AI output as a hypothesis generator and documents it that way, I think we'll find a lot of common ground. If people try to present model predictions as surrogate evidence for safety, that's where you'll hit a wall, and honestly you should.

So my view is that the promise is real but it's front-loaded. AI compresses discovery and design. It raises the quality of what enters the clinic. And over time, as we accumulate better human data, the models will start to earn trust in the later stages too. But that trust has to be earned the same way everything else in medicine is, by showing it works in people.

r001.rationale: The response mentions the high clinical failure rate and says FDA safety is the right frame, but it does not say that the failure rate explains the FDA’s emphasis on safety.

r002.rationale: The response says models can “change the odds” by improving target selection and that AI raises the quality of what enters the clinic, clearly presenting improved chances of success as a promise of AI.

astra-6.text:
I think the promise is enormous, but we have to distinguish between designing a molecule and demonstrating that it’s a safe and effective medicine. AI can help you generate hypotheses, explore more possibilities, and decide which experiments to run. It doesn’t make the need for experimental validation go away.

The FDA’s emphasis on safety is appropriate. You’re giving an intervention to a person, and biology has a way of surprising you. A model’s prediction is useful evidence for what to test; it isn’t, by itself, evidence that a drug is safe.

What excites me is the feedback loop: better models helping us design better experiments, and those experiments generating data that improve the models. If we can identify failures earlier and understand more clearly which patients might benefit, that could make development both faster and safer. The goal is to get to reliable evidence more efficiently.

r001.rationale: The response says the FDA’s safety emphasis is appropriate because interventions can surprise us, but it does not attribute that emphasis to drug development’s high failure rate.

r002.rationale: The response describes faster, safer development and more efficient evidence gathering, but does not state that AI can increase the probability of success.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the promise is enormous, but we have to distinguish between generating a promising molecule and demonstrating that it’s safe and effective in a person. AI can help us search a much larger space of potential drugs, understand biology, and design better experiments. It doesn’t eliminate the need for experimental validation or clinical trials.

The opportunity is to build a tighter loop between computation and experiments: make a prediction, test it, learn from the result, and improve the next prediction. If that helps us identify failures earlier and understand which patients might benefit, that’s valuable for both drug development and safety. The goal should be better evidence, generated more efficiently.

r001.rationale: The response discusses safety but does not attribute the FDA’s emphasis on it to drug development’s high failure rate.

r002.rationale: The response describes AI helping identify failures earlier and improve evidence, but does not clearly say AI can increase the probability of drug development success.
